opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core use case we had in mind is what I'd call knowledge work that requires going out and gathering a lot of information, synthesizing it, and coming back with something you can actually act on. Think about the kinds of tasks where, today, you'd hand it to an analyst or a researcher and say, "Go spend a few hours, or maybe a few days, digging into this and come back with a report." Market research, competitive analysis, a literature review, understanding a technical topic you're new to, even things on the consumer side like researching which car to buy or planning a complicated trip.

What makes those tasks different from a normal chat interaction is that the answer usually isn't sitting in one place. You have to search, read a bunch of sources, figure out which ones are trustworthy, notice when something contradicts something else, follow a new thread when you discover you were asking the wrong question, and then pull it all together. That's a very iterative, multi-step process, and it's exactly the kind of thing that a model trained end to end with reinforcement learning on browsing and reasoning tasks can get good at.

So the way I think about it is: it's not meant to replace the quick question-and-answer experience. If you want a fast fact, regular chat with search is great. Deep Research is for when you're willing to wait five, ten, twenty minutes because the alternative is you spending hours doing it yourself. And the thing we optimized for is that the output is thorough, well cited, and something you can trust enough to actually build on, because you can go back and check every claim against the source.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research is for information-heavy tasks that need a thorough, actionable answer, distinguishing it from quick questions handled by regular chat.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is, Deep Research was really built for the kind of task where you'd otherwise go off and spend hours, or sometimes days, pulling together information from a bunch of different sources and synthesizing it into something coherent. So think about a market analysis, or a literature review, or trying to understand a technical topic that you're not an expert in and where the answer is spread across dozens of papers and blog posts and documentation pages. That's the sweet spot.

And I think the key insight behind it was that there's a class of problems where the value isn't really in any one answer. It's in the breadth of what you look at and the quality of how you connect it together. A traditional search engine gives you ten links and then the synthesis is on you. A chatbot gives you a quick answer from what the model happens to remember. Deep Research sits in a different spot, where the agent is actually going out, browsing, reading, deciding what to read next based on what it just learned, and then coming back with a report that has citations you can check.

So I'd say the design target was the knowledge worker who has a genuinely hard research question, where they'd be willing to wait five, ten, thirty minutes to get something that's actually thorough rather than something instant and shallow. And part of what made it interesting from an engineering standpoint is that this is one of the first places where the agentic framing, where the model takes many steps and uses tools and reasons about what to do next, really started to pay off in a way that users could feel. The longer time horizon is a feature, not a bug, because it's buying you depth.

What we found is that people use it for things we expected, like due diligence and competitive analysis, but also a lot of personal stuff, like researching a major purchase or a medical question or planning something complicated. Anywhere the alternative is a lot of tabs open and a lot of manual note-taking.

r001.rationale: The response describes Deep Research as suited to lengthy, thorough research and contrasts it with search engines and quick chatbot answers, but does not say it is for getting a more thorough answer when that need arises during ordinary ChatGPT use.

astra-6.text: I think the use case is pretty straightforward: you have a question that would take you hours to research yourself. You’d have to search for information, read a bunch of sources, follow up on things you find, and then synthesize that into an answer. Deep Research is designed to take on that longer workflow. So instead of giving you an immediate response, it spends time investigating and comes back with a report that you can inspect and follow the sources for. The value is in doing that legwork on a question where a quick answer isn’t really enough.

r001.rationale: The response describes Deep Research as handling questions that require extensive investigation and producing a sourced report, but it does not say this need arises during ordinary ChatGPT use.

sol-6.1.text: I think the use case Deep Research was designed for is taking a question that would otherwise require you to spend hours going through sources, comparing information, and synthesizing it into a report, and doing a lot of that work for you. You give it a fairly high-level objective, and it figures out what to search for, follows up on what it finds, and pulls the results together. So it’s useful when you don’t just need a quick answer—you need to build an understanding of a topic or make a decision based on information from a bunch of different places.

r001.rationale: The response describes using Deep Research for thorough, source-based answers, but does not say this need arises during ordinary ChatGPT use.
